local.title: Beds around older homes need **a reset, not a pile.**
local.intro: Most beds in the city hug houses built before 1960, and many have had mulch dumped on them every spring for years. The bed creeps up the siding, the edge disappears into the lawn and the tree in the corner ends up in a mulch volcano. Fresh mulch works best once the old buildup is sorted out.

points.title: Right depth, off the trunk
points.body: MSU Extension says 2 to 3 inches of mulch is enough and more is not better, and it warns against piling mulch against trunks. If old layers have built up, we rake them down before anything new goes on.

points.title: An edge you can see
points.body: If your bed has an old brick border that has sunk, or a line that has wandered into the lawn, we cut a clean natural edge or set a gray block border, so the mulch stays in and the mower stays out.

points.title: Beds by the walk and the drive
points.body: Beds along the walk and the driveway catch salty snow all winter, and MSU notes salt can damage plants through spray and buildup in the soil. Come spring, those are often the beds that need the most help.

points.title: The strip between walk and street
points.body: Before anyone digs a new bed in the strip by the street, the city wants a right of way permit, and the street tree there is the city's to look after. Mulch work stays on your side of the walk unless the city says otherwise.

logistics.title: How a mulch job runs at a Flint house.
body: Rob walks the beds with you and talks color: black, brown or red. He checks how deep the old mulch is, where the edge has gone and whether the bed should have fabric, then gives you a price.
On the day, we weed, cut or reset the edge, lay fabric where it helps, and wheelbarrow fresh mulch in from the trailer. The walk and the drive get blown clean before we pull away.

Spring is when most people want fresh mulch, and fall works too, once the leaves are cleared. Bigger changes, like new block walls or a full replant, are a [landscaping job in Flint](/landscaping-flint-mi/).

faq.q: Do you install mulch in Flint, MI?
faq.a: Yes. Grand Scapes installs mulch in Flint: beds weeded, edged, laid with fabric where it helps and covered in fresh black, brown or red mulch. Rob looks at the beds first and quotes a price, and the estimate is free.

About 2 to 3 inches. MSU Extension says more is not better, and mulch piled against a trunk creates a damp spot that invites rot and insects. If old mulch has built up, we rake it down before the new layer goes on.

faq.q: Which mulch color goes with an older brick house?
faq.a: It depends on the brick and the plants. Black makes green leaves and gray block stand out, brown reads natural against red brick, and red suits some homes. Rob can talk it through standing at the bed with you.

faq.q: Do you put landscape fabric under mulch?
faq.a: Where it helps, yes. Fabric under mulch slows weeds in beds of shrubs and perennials. In a bed where you plant annuals every year it gets in the way, so Rob will tell you which beds should have it.

faq.q: Can you redo the edges and mulch in one visit?
faq.a: Yes, and that is the right order: edge first, then mulch. A crisp edge is what makes new mulch look finished, and it keeps the mulch from washing into the lawn.
